definition: A nonwoven is a sheet or web of fibers or filaments bonded by mechanical, thermal or chemical means rather than by weaving, knitting or interlacing yarns, used in hygiene, filtration, geotextile and apparel products.
explanation: Nonwoven manufacture has two stages, web formation and bonding. Webs are formed dry (carding or airlaying staple fiber), wet (from a papermaking-style slurry) or directly from polymer (spunbond and meltblown). Bonding then gives strength. Needlepunching drives barbed needles through the web to entangle fibers mechanically. Spunlacing, or hydroentanglement, uses fine, high-pressure water jets to give a soft, textile-like fabric common in wipes. Thermal bonding fuses thermoplastic fibers at points or throughout, and chemical bonding uses binders. Many products stack layers, such as spunbond-meltblown-spunbond (SMS) composites.
example: A student takes apart a disposable face mask. The outer and inner layers are spunbond polypropylene with a regular pattern of bond points visible under a lens; the middle layer is meltblown, much finer and softer, and does most of the filtering. None of the layers contains yarn, yet each behaves as a fabric suited to its job.
caution: Nonwoven describes construction, not fiber content or durability; nonwovens range from single-use wipes to long-lived geotextiles. Some contain cellulose and may be marketed as biodegradable, but many wipes include polyester or polypropylene, so check fiber content. Wet-felted wool is sometimes grouped with nonwovens, but its cohesion comes from fiber scales rather than an engineered bonding step.
deeper: Spunbond lines melt spin continuous filaments, draw them with high-velocity air, lay them randomly on a moving belt and usually bond them by calendering between heated, patterned rolls. Meltblown lines attenuate molten polymer with hot, high-velocity air into filaments much finer than spunbond; the large fiber surface area suits filtration, and electret charging improves capture efficiency and its durability. Polyolefin spunbond and meltblown fabrics dominate disposable hygiene and medical products. Thermal bonding of staple webs often uses core-sheath bicomponent binder fibers whose low-softening sheath fuses at crossings. Needlepunched strength rises with needle density and penetration depth, and hydroentanglement forces water through small orifices at high pressure to wrap fibers around one another. Basis weight, fiber orientation and bond pattern tune the final properties.
origins: Felt made from wool is often cited as a forerunner, but the modern nonwoven industry grew in the twentieth century, drawing on textile carding, papermaking and, later, polymer extrusion. Bicomponent binder fibers, commercialized from the 1960s, broadened thermal bonding, and spunbond and meltblown lines turned polymer directly into fabric. A review of melt-spun fibers reports that nonwovens now account for the largest tonnage among technical textiles. The name still defines the category by exclusion, as fabrics made without weaving or knitting.

definition: A statement that a product contains a stated share of organically grown fiber, usually supported by a chain-of-custody standard such as Textile Exchange's Organic Content Standard.
explanation: Organic status belongs to how a crop or animal was raised and is certified at the farm under a recognized organic regulation. After the fiber leaves the farm, a content claim depends on tracking that material through ginning, spinning, fabric production and garment assembly. Textile Exchange's Organic Content Standard (OCS) provides voluntary third-party certification of that chain of custody. It has two label grades: OCS 100 for products with at least 95 percent organic material, and OCS Blended for products with at least 5 percent, measured against the total product excluding accessories and trims.
example: A T-shirt fabric is 60 percent organic cotton and 40 percent conventional polyester. Under the OCS framework it could only carry the Blended grade, and the claim would state the organic percentage. A student evaluating the shirt should ask for the relevant certificates and transaction documentation, and should notice that the claim says nothing about how the fabric was dyed or finished.
caution: An organic content claim describes where the fiber came from, not the chemistry of processing or conditions in factories. OCS is a content and chain-of-custody standard; it is not designed to set criteria for dyes, finishes, wastewater or labor, whereas GOTS adds environmental and social criteria for processing. Organic farming also permits certain approved inputs, so organic does not mean that no substances were ever applied.
deeper: OCS certification applies to each site that handles the material, from the first processor through manufacturing, packaging, labeling, storage and shipping, up to the seller in the final business-to-business transaction. Farm certification sits outside OCS itself: the fiber must come from farms certified to recognized national organic standards, which in the United States means the USDA National Organic Program for agricultural production. The claim percentage is calculated by weight on the whole product minus accessories and trims. Laboratory screens for genetically modified cotton DNA or pesticide residues can flag problems, but no test can prove organic origin, so documentary evidence, including scope certificates, transaction certificates and audited volume reconciliation, carries the claim.
origins: Textile Exchange, which began as Organic Exchange, developed the Organic Content Standard to give organic fiber claims a common chain-of-custody basis; the standard carries a 2013 copyright, and version 3.0 is dated 1 March 2020. Its two-grade structure, a near-complete grade and a blended grade with a low minimum, mirrors the approach of Textile Exchange's Recycled Claim Standard.

definition: Plain weave is the simplest interlacing, in which each weft passes alternately over one warp end and under the next, reversing on every pick.
explanation: The repeat is only two ends by two picks, and every yarn changes sides at every opportunity. This gives the highest possible number of interlacings, a firm structure and identical faces. Variations keep the alternating principle but group yarns: a basket or hopsack weave moves two or more yarns together, and a rib weave uses a heavier or doubled yarn in one direction. Poplin, percale, voile, chiffon and taffeta are all plain weaves differing mainly in yarn and density.
example: Hold a plain-woven cotton poplin and a twill chino up to light. The poplin shows a regular grid with no diagonal line, and both faces look nearly identical. Cut a small square and pull out a few yarns from each: the poplin's yarns show a tight, even crimp because they bend around a crossing yarn at every intersection, while the twill's yarns have longer straight runs.
caution: Plain weave describes interlacing only. It says nothing about fiber, yarn count, thread count or weight. Sheer voile and heavy canvas are both plain weaves. A plain weave is not automatically durable or breathable, and its frequent interlacings can make it stiffer and more prone to tearing than a looser twill of similar weight.
deeper: In weave notation plain weave is written 1/1: one up, one down. With one interlacing per yarn crossing, floats are as short as possible, so yarns are gripped tightly and crimp is high. High crimp increases extensibility along the yarn direction under low load and affects shrinkage behavior. Because yarns cannot slide together, tear load is shared by fewer yarns at the tear tip, so plain weaves tend to show lower tear strength than twills of similar specification. Experimental comparisons of 1/1 plain, 2/2 twill and 8-end satin fabrics woven from the same yarns report significant differences in stiffness and tensile behavior, with float length identified as a controlling factor.
origins: Plain weave needs only two alternating sheds, so it can be produced on the simplest looms with two groups of heddles. That mechanical simplicity explains why it underlies many unrelated weaving traditions and why so many fabric names, from calico to taffeta, are plain weaves distinguished by fiber and finish. The alternative name tabby is used particularly in handweaving and textile history.
